z-m-20-01.title: Is the sum of two quadratic expressions always a quadratic expression?
z-m-20-01.topic: Degree of a polynomial: adding and multiplying
z-m-20-01.goal: Explain how the degree changes in the sum and the product of polynomials, telling the cases apart with counterexamples and reasons.
z-m-20-01.material: Polynomials A and B are both quadratic expressions in x. That means the coefficient of x² is not 0 (read: x² is "x squared"), and all coefficients are real numbers. The degree is the degree of the highest term whose coefficient is not 0. For example, x²+3x is a quadratic expression and 2 has degree 0. We will not consider the case where A+B or A−B is 0 itself. Seoyeon said, "If you add quadratic expressions, you get a quadratic expression, and if you multiply them, you get a degree-4 expression."
z-m-20-01.thinking.0: Testing the claim "always" with a counterexample
z-m-20-01.thinking.1: Compare the sum and the product and reason about which one can lose its highest-degree term
z-m-20-01.thinking.2: Design your own examples that satisfy the conditions
z-m-20-01.prereq.0: H1 in this task only marks the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it is not a grade placement in the curriculum. Assume you know middle school polynomial addition, subtraction and multiplication, the multiplication formulas, and basic factoring.
z-m-20-01.prereq.1: The meaning of the degree and the highest-degree term of a polynomial
z-m-20-01.prereq.2: The product of two nonzero numbers is not 0
z-m-20-01.s.s1.prompt: When A and B are quadratic expressions satisfying the condition above, choose all the statements that are always true no matter which two quadratic expressions you pick.
z-m-20-01.s.s1.hint.0: If a statement is always true, it must hold for any pair of quadratic expressions you plug in. Pick two simple quadratic expressions, add them and multiply them, and check the degree.
z-m-20-01.s.s1.hint.1: Try choosing the x² coefficients on purpose to see whether you can break a and d.
z-m-20-01.s.s1.o.a: A+B is always a quadratic expression.
z-m-20-01.s.s1.r.a: You said "always" without testing the case where the sum of the x² coefficients is 0.
z-m-20-01.s.s1.o.b: The degree of A+B does not exceed 2.
z-m-20-01.s.s1.r.b: This judgment sees that adding only adds the coefficients of terms of the same degree, so no new higher-degree term appears.
z-m-20-01.s.s1.o.c: A×B is always a degree-4 expression.
z-m-20-01.s.s1.r.c: This judgment considers which two terms multiply to make the highest-degree term of the product.
z-m-20-01.s.s1.o.d: The degree of A−B is always less than 2.
z-m-20-01.s.s1.r.d: You thought the highest-degree term disappears when you subtract. It disappears only when the two x² coefficients are equal. For example, if A=x² and B=2x², then A−B=−x².
z-m-20-01.s.s1.r.e: You carried over what happens in the sum to the product as it is. Think about how the coefficient of the highest-degree term of the product is made.
z-m-20-01.s.s1.explain: b and c hold for any pair of quadratic expressions. a breaks when the sum of the two x² coefficients is 0, and d breaks when the two x² coefficients are different. Why e does not hold is something you will explain yourself in the last step.
z-m-20-01.s.s2.hint.0: First write how the coefficient of the x² term in A+B can be expressed using a and c.
z-m-20-01.s.s2.hint.1: Choose a so that this coefficient becomes 0 and match c to it. Then pick b and d freely and add to check.
z-m-20-01.s.s2.var.a: The x² coefficient a of A
z-m-20-01.s.s2.var.b: The x coefficient b of A
z-m-20-01.s.s2.var.c: The x² coefficient c of B
z-m-20-01.s.s2.var.d: The x coefficient d of B
z-m-20-01.s.s2.fail.c1: If the x² coefficient a of A is 0, then A is not a quadratic expression.
z-m-20-01.s.s2.fail.c2: If the x² coefficient c of B is 0, then B is not a quadratic expression.
z-m-20-01.s.s2.ok.c3: No x² term is left in A+B.
z-m-20-01.s.s2.fail.c3: There is still an x² term left in A+B. Find the x² coefficient of A+B and check.
z-m-20-01.s.s2.explain: For example, if A=x²+2x+1 and B=−x²+5x+2, then A+B=7x+3, which is a linear expression. If A=2x²+3x+1 and B=−2x²+3x+2, then A+B=6x+3. Both expressions are quadratic, but if the sum of the x² coefficients is 0, the sum is not a quadratic expression. So "adding quadratic expressions gives a quadratic expression" is not always true.
z-m-20-01.s.s3.prompt: Of Seoyeon's claims, "adding gives a quadratic expression" was broken, but "multiplying gives a degree-4 expression" was not. Write in your own words why the highest-degree term cannot disappear in the product, comparing it with the sum.
z-m-20-01.s.s3.hint.0: Find which term of A and which term of B must be multiplied to make the x⁴ term in A×B.
z-m-20-01.s.s3.hint.1: The x² coefficient of A+B is a+c. Write how the x⁴ coefficient of A×B appears, and compare the two.
z-m-20-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: In the sum ... but in the product ...
z-m-20-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write in your own words why the highest-degree term can disappear in the sum (the coefficients add up to 0)?
z-m-20-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write which two terms multiply to make the highest-degree term of the product?
z-m-20-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you use the fact that the product of two nonzero numbers is not 0 as a reason?
z-m-20-01.s.s3.model.0: In the sum, we add the x² coefficients, and a+c can be 0, so the x² term can disappear. In the product, the coefficient of the highest-degree term is ac, the product of a and c. If a and c are both nonzero, ac is not 0 either, so the x⁴ term always stays.
z-m-20-01.s.s3.model.1: When we multiply, the product of the highest-degree terms is the x⁴ term, and that is the only product that makes an x⁴ term, so no other term cancels it. The coefficient is also a product of nonzero numbers, so it is not 0. In a sum, + and − can meet and make 0, so a term can disappear, but that cannot happen in a product.
z-m-20-01.s.s3.model.2: For example, in (x²+1)(−x²+2), the only x⁴ term is x²×(−x²)=−x⁴, and its coefficient −1 is not 0, so it is a degree-4 expression. In the sum (x²+1)+(−x²+2), the x² coefficient is 1+(−1)=0, so the x² term disappeared.
z-m-20-01.s.s3.modelNote.2: An answer explained with specific expressions is also valid.

z-m-20-02.title: Which expression has a value that is fixed by the sum alone?
z-m-20-02.topic: Multiplication formulas and values of expressions: two numbers with a given sum
z-m-20-02.goal: Decide which expression has a single value when only the sum a+b of two numbers is known, and tell apart extra information that is enough from information that is not enough to fix the value.
z-m-20-02.material: For two real numbers a and b, all you know is that a+b=6. Nothing says that a and b are integers, and nothing says they are positive. We want to see which expression values we can find without finding a and b separately. Reading: a² is "a squared", ab is "a times b", and a³ is "a cubed".
z-m-20-02.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-20-02.thinking.1: Making your own counterexamples (same sum, different values)
z-m-20-02.thinking.2: Comparing how sufficient extra pieces of information are
z-m-20-02.thinking.3: Explaining a conditional conclusion (the square is fixed but the sign is not)
z-m-20-02.prereq.0: H1 in this task only marks the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it is not a grade placement in the curriculum. Assume you know middle school polynomial addition, subtraction and multiplication, the multiplication formulas, and basic factoring.
z-m-20-02.prereq.3: Experience transforming expressions without finding the values of the real numbers a and b separately
z-m-20-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the expressions whose value is fixed to a single value by the fact a+b=6 alone.
z-m-20-02.s.s1.hint.0: For each expression you choose, plug in two different pairs (a, b) that satisfy a+b=6 and compare whether the values are the same.
z-m-20-02.s.s1.hint.1: For the expressions whose values are the same, check whether you can group them so that a+b appears in the expression as it is.
z-m-20-02.s.s1.r.a: The value can change depending on how a and b split the sum, and you did not test that. Plug in a=3, b=3 and a=0, b=6 and compare.
z-m-20-02.s.s1.r.b: This judgment sees that the sum a+b is contained in the expression as one chunk.
z-m-20-02.s.s1.r.c: Even with the same sum, the sign of the difference can change depending on whether a is larger or b is larger, and you missed that.
z-m-20-02.s.s1.r.d: This judgment recognized the expression as the form of a multiplication formula.
z-m-20-02.s.s1.r.e: 2a+2b is fixed but a²+b² is not, so the sum is not fixed either. You thought that if one part is fixed, the whole is fixed.
z-m-20-02.s.s1.explain: 2a+2b=2(a+b)=12 and a²+2ab+b²=(a+b)²=36. a²+b² is 18 if a=3, b=3 and 36 if a=0, b=6, so it is not fixed. a−b is also 2 if a=4, b=2 and −2 if a=2, b=4.
z-m-20-02.s.s2.prompt: Make three pairs (a, b) with a+b=6 for which the values of a²+b² are all different. (a, b) and (b, a) count as the same pair.
z-m-20-02.s.s2.hint.0: First choose a, set b to 6−a, and then calculate a²+b² directly.
z-m-20-02.s.s2.hint.1: To see whether the values differ, choose different values for a, such as 0, 1, 2, and compare.
z-m-20-02.s.s2.fail.c1: a+b is not 6. Add the two numbers and check.
z-m-20-02.s.s2.explain: For (1, 5), a²+b²=26; for (2, 4), it is 20; for (3, 3), it is 18; and for (0, 6), it is 36. Even with the same sum, the values of a²+b² are different. (1, 5) and (5, 1) have the same a²+b², so they count as the same example.
z-m-20-02.s.s3.prompt: In addition to a+b=6, which of the conditions below would fix the value of a²+b² to a single value? Choose all that are enough. (a and b are real numbers)
z-m-20-02.s.s3.hint.0: For each option, think about whether that condition together with a+b=6 lets you find a, b, or ab.
z-m-20-02.s.s3.hint.1: For a condition that does not narrow the candidates down to one, check whether two pairs with different a²+b² (for example, (1, 5) and (2, 4)) both satisfy that condition.
z-m-20-02.s.s3.r.a: If a is an integer, many possibilities remain, such as a=1 and a=2, and you did not test whether the value is fixed.
z-m-20-02.s.s3.r.b: This judgment sees that if you know both the sum and the product, you can express a²+b² using the sum and the product.
z-m-20-02.s.s3.o.c: a and b are both positive
z-m-20-02.s.s3.r.c: A sign condition reduces the candidates but does not narrow them down to one. a=1, b=5 and a=2, b=4 are both positive.
z-m-20-02.s.s3.r.d: This judgment uses the fact that if you know a+b and a−b, you can find a and b separately.
z-m-20-02.s.s3.r.e: This judgment sees that the sum of cubes can also be expressed with the sum and the product, so the product ab can be found.
z-m-20-02.s.s3.explain: If ab=8, then a²+b²=(a+b)²−2ab=36−16=20. If a−b=2, then a=4 and b=2, so it is 20. From a³+b³=(a+b)³−3ab(a+b)=216−18ab=144, we get ab=4, so a²+b²=36−8=28. A condition like being an integer or being positive only reduces the candidates and does not narrow them to one.
z-m-20-02.s.s4.prompt: When a+b=6 and ab=8, a friend said, "a−b is also fixed to a single value." Do you agree? Write your answer with reasons.
z-m-20-02.s.s4.hint.0: Find two specific numbers whose sum is 6 and whose product is 8, and calculate a−b.
z-m-20-02.s.s4.hint.1: Compare what happens to a−b if you swap the names a and b of the two numbers you found.
z-m-20-02.s.s4.placeholder: Example: If a+b=6 and ab=8, then ...
z-m-20-02.s.s4.selfAssess.0: Did you give a reason by stating what (a−b)² is, or by using specific pairs like a=4, b=2 and a=2, b=4?
z-m-20-02.s.s4.selfAssess.1: Did you clearly write that a−b can have two values (the sign)?
z-m-20-02.s.s4.selfAssess.2: Did you distinguish that the square (a−b)² is fixed but a−b itself is not fixed?
z-m-20-02.s.s4.model.0: I do not agree. (a−b)²=(a+b)²−4ab=36−32=4, so a−b is 2 or −2. Which one it is depends on the order of a and b, so it is not fixed to one value.
z-m-20-02.s.s4.model.1: If a=4, b=2, then a−b=2, and if a=2, b=4, then a−b=−2, and in both cases the sum is 6 and the product is 8. So a−b is not fixed to one value, and only the square (a−b)²=4 is fixed.
z-m-20-02.s.s4.model.2: Only the absolute value 2 is fixed. Even if the sum and the product are the same, swapping a and b changes the sign of a−b, so −2 is also possible, and it is not just one value.

z-m-20-03.title: Designing a degree-4 expression that is a product of four linear expressions
z-m-20-03.topic: Factoring and designing degree-4 expressions using substitution
z-m-20-03.goal: Compare plans for splitting a degree-4 expression with a repeated chunk, design expressions that are products of four linear expressions by yourself, and explain why the conditions are needed.
z-m-20-03.material: The expression (x²+x)²−8(x²+x)+12 can be written as a product of four linear expressions with integer coefficients (reading: the square of x squared plus x, minus 8 times x squared plus x, plus 12). It is fine for the same linear expression to repeat. Among the similar expressions (x²+x)²+m(x²+x)+n (m and n are integers), we want to find some that are products of four linear expressions with integer coefficients.
z-m-20-03.thinking.0: Picking out the valid ones among several solution plans
z-m-20-03.thinking.1: Designing several expressions that satisfy the constraints
z-m-20-03.thinking.2: Generalizing and explaining the condition for splitting
z-m-20-03.prereq.0: H1 in this task only marks the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it is not a grade placement in the curriculum. Assume you know middle school polynomial addition, subtraction and multiplication, the multiplication formulas, and basic factoring.
z-m-20-03.prereq.1: Factoring quadratic expressions of the form x²+px+q (thinking in terms of a sum and a product)
z-m-20-03.prereq.2: Experience of replacing a chunk with one letter to look at an expression
z-m-20-03.prereq.3: The meaning of a linear expression with integer coefficients
z-m-20-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the plans that can be carried through to the end to write the given expression (x²+x)²−8(x²+x)+12 as a product of linear expressions with integer coefficients.
z-m-20-03.s.s1.hint.0: Follow each plan for a line or two and check whether four linear expressions come out at the end.
z-m-20-03.s.s1.o.a: Plug in some integers for x, and if 0 never comes out, decide that it cannot be split
z-m-20-03.s.s1.r.a: You concluded that it cannot be split just because 0 did not come out for a few values. You may have missed a candidate, or missed that it can split into quadratic expressions rather than linear ones.
z-m-20-03.s.s1.o.b: Replace x²+x with one letter and split it like a quadratic expression, then look at the two resulting expressions again
z-m-20-03.s.s1.r.b: This is a plan to treat the repeated chunk as one and solve in steps.
z-m-20-03.s.s1.o.c: Write (x−2)(x−6) and give it as the answer without putting x²+x in the place of x
z-m-20-03.s.s1.r.c: You missed that x²+x must go in the place of the chunk. Look at which place has to be restored for the quadratic expression in one letter to become the same expression as the original.
z-m-20-03.s.s1.o.d: Expand all the parentheses into a degree-4 expression, then plug in divisors of 12 and start with the ones that give 0
z-m-20-03.s.s1.r.d: This is a plan to systematically test factor candidates in the expanded expression.
z-m-20-03.s.s1.explain: Both b and d can be carried through to the end. b splits into something like (A−2)(A−6), then restores A=x²+x and splits again, and d solves it as a degree-4 expression and finds the factors one by one with the factor theorem. a did not test all the candidates, and c did not restore the letter.
z-m-20-03.s.s2.prompt: Find two different integer pairs (m, n) for which (x²+x)²+m(x²+x)+n is a product of four linear expressions with integer coefficients. However, n is not 0, and exclude (m, n)=(−8, 12) above.
z-m-20-03.s.s2.hint.0: Treat x²+x as one letter, choose p and q so that it takes the form (that letter−p)(that letter−q), and then find m=−(p+q) and n=pq.
z-m-20-03.s.s2.hint.1: For the p and q you chose, check separately whether x²+x−p and x²+x−q each split into two linear expressions with integer coefficients.
z-m-20-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Please take m and n to be integers.
z-m-20-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The quadratic expression that treats x²+x as one letter satisfies the discriminant condition for having integer roots.
z-m-20-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The quadratic expression that treats x²+x as one letter does not split into two linear expressions with integer coefficients.
z-m-20-03.s.s2.ok.c3: That quadratic expression splits into two expressions with integer coefficients.
z-m-20-03.s.s2.fail.c3: That quadratic expression does not split into two expressions with integer coefficients.
z-m-20-03.s.s2.ok.c4: The two split expressions split again into linear expressions with integer coefficients.
z-m-20-03.s.s2.fail.c4: At least one of the two expressions from the first split does not split further into two linear expressions with integer coefficients.
z-m-20-03.s.s2.ok.c6: It is different from the given example.
z-m-20-03.s.s2.fail.c6: (m, n)=(−8, 12) is already the given example.
z-m-20-03.s.s2.explain: For example, if (m, n)=(−14, 24), then (x²+x−2)(x²+x−12)=(x+2)(x−1)(x+4)(x−3), and if (−18, 72), then (x²+x−6)(x²+x−12)=(x+3)(x−2)(x+4)(x−3). If (−4, 4), then (x²+x−2)²=(x+2)²(x−1)². (−5, 6) splits into (x²+x−2)(x²+x−3), but x²+x−3 does not split further into linear expressions with integer coefficients.
z-m-20-03.s.s3.prompt: If (m, n)=(−4, 3), it splits into (x²+x−3)(x²+x−1). Does x²+x−3 among these split further into a product of two linear expressions with integer coefficients? Answer "it splits" or "it does not split" and write the reason.
z-m-20-03.s.s3.hint.0: Let x²+x−3=(x+u)(x+v) and write how the coefficient of x and the constant term come out in terms of u and v when you expand the right side.
z-m-20-03.s.s3.hint.1: List all the integer pairs whose product is −3, find the sum of each, and check whether any of them is 1.
z-m-20-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write what u+v and uv must each be when written in the form (x+u)(x+v)?
z-m-20-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write whether you looked for such integers u and v (or gave another reason, such as the discriminant)?
z-m-20-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you state whether the conclusion "it does not work" comes from checking a number of candidates or from some condition?
z-m-20-03.s.s3.model.0: It does not split. If we write it as (x+u)(x+v), we need u+v=1 and uv=−3, but the integer pairs with product −3 are only (1, −3) and (−1, 3), and their sums are −2 and 2, so we cannot get 1.
z-m-20-03.s.s3.model.1: It does not split further with integer coefficients. The discriminant of x²+x−3=0 is 1+12=13, and 13 is not a perfect square, so the roots are neither integers nor fractions, and then it cannot be written as a product of two linear expressions with integer coefficients.
z-m-20-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: An explanation using the discriminant is also valid.
z-m-20-03.s.s3.model.2: When p=2, there are u=2 and v=−1 with sum 1 and product −2, so it splits. But for 3, there is no integer pair with product −3 and sum 1, so it does not split. So it seems that p has to be a product of two consecutive integers, like 2, 6, 12, for it to split.

z-m-20-04.title: Is the value of an expression with an irrational number plugged in an irrational number?
z-m-20-04.topic: The value and the remainder of an expression with an irrational number plugged in
z-m-20-04.goal: Check by calculation that the value of a cubic expression with an irrational number plugged in can be an integer, and make another expression with value 4 for the same reason.
z-m-20-04.material: We want to find out the value of E=x³−3x²−3x+5 when x=2+√3. Reading: x is "2 plus root 3" and x³ is "x cubed". We do not use a calculator. √3 is the positive number whose square is 3, and it cannot be written as a fraction. Information is revealed one piece at a time, so each time choose what you think is most fitting right now.
z-m-20-04.thinking.0: Revising your guess from before the calculation each time more information appears
z-m-20-04.thinking.1: Generalizing the reason for the result
z-m-20-04.thinking.2: Designing several expressions with the same property
z-m-20-04.prereq.0: H1 in this task only marks the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it is not a grade placement in the curriculum. Assume you know middle school polynomial addition, subtraction and multiplication, the multiplication formulas, and basic factoring.
z-m-20-04.prereq.1: The fact that √3×√3=3 and that √3 cannot be written as a fraction
z-m-20-04.prereq.2: Adding, subtracting and multiplying numbers of the form (a+b√3)
z-m-20-04.prereq.3: The meaning of the quotient and remainder when a polynomial is divided by a polynomial (the division expression A=BQ+R)
z-m-20-04.s.s1.prompt: Each time information is revealed, choose what you think about the value of E.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write how far you can go with only the calculations known so far.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.hint.1: Test the statements with "must" or "never" among the options by using counterexamples or calculation.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.0.info: x is the irrational number 2+√3, and E has terms where x is multiplied several times (x³, x²). All you have calculated so far is x²=(2+√3)²=7+4√3.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: What form do you think the value of E will take?
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.0.after: You can make a guess, but you do not yet have a basis to say it must be irrational. If you calculate up to x³, you will be able to tell.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Since x is irrational, I am almost sure E is also irrational.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: When you calculate with irrational numbers, √3 can cancel out. For example, (1+√3)+(1−√3)=2. It is too early to say "must" before calculating.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It looks likely to be irrational, but we only know for sure after calculating up to x³.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You made a guess and also thought about the need to check it.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: All the coefficients of the expression are integers, so E is an integer even without calculating.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The fact that the coefficients are integers does not give the same conclusion as when x is an integer.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: I only know x², so x³ is hard to find, and I think nothing can be said for now.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You can continue with x³=x²×x. You can keep calculating with the information you have now.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.info: x³=x²×x=(7+4√3)(2+√3)=26+15√3. Put x²=7+4√3, x=2+√3, x³=26+15√3 into E=x³−3x²−3x+5, and collect the integer part and the coefficient of √3 separately.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: What can you say about the value of E?
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.after: The integer part is 26−21−6+5=4 and the coefficient of √3 is 15−12−3=0. So E=4. Even if you plug in the irrational number x, the value can be an integer, and if you first guessed "it is likely irrational", you need to revise that guess.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The coefficient of √3 becomes 15−12−3=0, so E is the integer 4.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This judgment comes from collecting the two parts separately.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: A √3 term remains, so E is irrational.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You did not collect all the coefficients of the √3 terms and looked only at 15. Calculate 15−12−3.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The coefficient of √3 is 0, so the whole E is 0.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: The √3 term disappearing is different from the integer part being 0. Also calculate the integer part 26−21−6+5.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Since x is irrational, this calculation result cannot be trusted either.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: A calculation with an irrational number plugged in is also exact. A result being an integer does not make it wrong.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.2.info: x=2+√3 satisfies x²−4x+1=0 (x²=7+4√3 and 4x=8+4√3, so x²−4x+1=0). Also, when E is divided by x²−4x+1, the quotient is x+1 and the remainder is 4, so E=(x+1)(x²−4x+1)+4 holds.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the value if you plug x=2−√3 into E? (2−√3 also satisfies x²−4x+1=0. You can also check by plugging it in directly.)
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.2.after: If x²−4x+1=0 holds, then E=(x+1)×0+4=4. 2−√3 satisfies the same equation, so the value is the same. If you plug it in directly, you also get 4.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The sign of √3 changed, so the sign of the integer part will change too and it will be −4.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Only the √3 term changes sign. See what happens to the integer part 4.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: In E=(x+1)(x²−4x+1)+4, x²−4x+1=0, so it is 4.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This judgment uses the structure of the expression.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: I plugged in a number different from 2+√3, so the calculated value will also be different.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Plugging in a different number can still give the same value. Look at the role x²−4x+1 plays in the division expression.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: I cannot know until I plug in and calculate directly, so I will calculate x³ and x².
z-m-20-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This is a plan to check directly. It shows that there is more than one way to reach the answer.
z-m-20-04.s.s1.reflect: At first you guessed that E would be irrational. After seeing the calculation result, how did that guess change? What did the second piece of information and the third piece of information each tell you?
z-m-20-04.s.s2.prompt: Make two different cubic expressions x³+ax²+bx+c (a, b, c are integers) whose value is 4 when x=2+√3. However, exclude the expression with a=−3 (the E above).
z-m-20-04.s.s2.hint.0: Using x³=26+15√3, x²=7+4√3, x=2+√3 for x=2+√3, write the value of x³+ax²+bx+c in the form (integer part)+(coefficient of √3)√3.
z-m-20-04.s.s2.hint.1: First choose a so that the coefficient of √3 becomes 0 and the integer part becomes 4, and then match b and c.
z-m-20-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Please take a, b, c to be integers.
z-m-20-04.s.s2.ok.c2: In the value with x=2+√3 plugged in, there is no part with √3 attached.
z-m-20-04.s.s2.fail.c2: In the value with x=2+√3 plugged in, a part with √3 attached remains. Use x³=26+15√3 and x²=7+4√3 to collect the coefficient of √3.
z-m-20-04.s.s2.fail.c3: The integer part is not 4. Collect the integer parts and check.
z-m-20-04.s.s2.ok.c4: It is different from the given E.
z-m-20-04.s.s2.fail.c4: a=−3 is the E above (or the same expression).
z-m-20-04.s.s2.explain: For example, if you plug x=2+√3 into x³−15x+8, you get 26+15√3−30−15√3+8=4. x³+x²−19x+9 and x³−2x²−7x+6 also give 4. All of these expressions differ from E only by a multiple of x²−4x+1.
z-m-20-04.s.s3.prompt: Choose one of the expressions you made and write why its value is the same 4 when x=2−√3, not only when x=2+√3. You may explain with a direct substitution calculation, or you may explain using x²−4x+1.
z-m-20-04.s.s3.hint.0: For the expression you chose, find x³, x², and x at x=2−√3 and write each split into an integer part and a √3 part.
z-m-20-04.s.s3.hint.1: Compare with the calculation you used for x=2+√3 and find the terms whose sign alone changed.
z-m-20-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The expression I chose is ..., so ...

z-m-20-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why it also holds at x=2−√3, using a calculation or a property like x²−4x+1=0?
z-m-20-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say separately how the integer part 4 and the √3 part 0 each came out?
z-m-20-04.s.s3.model.0: For x³−15x+8, when x=2−√3, x²=7−4√3 and x³=26−15√3, so 26−15√3−15(2−√3)+8=4. The −15√3 and +15√3 attached to √3 cancel each other, and the integer part is 26−30+8=4.
z-m-20-04.s.s3.model.1: This expression can be written in the form (x−4)(x²−4x+1)+4. 2+√3 and 2−√3 both satisfy x²−4x+1=0, so the first part becomes 0 and only 4 is left.
z-m-20-04.s.s3.model.2: Since x²=4x−1, x³=4x²−x=15x−4. When I put this into my expression, the part unrelated to √3 is fixed as 4, so whichever of the values I plug in for x, it is the same 4.
z-m-20-04.s.s3.modelNote.2: This is a method of lowering the degree by repeatedly using x²=4x−1.

z-m-20-05.title: What can we know about the coefficients without expanding?
z-m-20-05.topic: Finding sums of coefficients by plugging in values of x
z-m-20-05.goal: Without expanding the expression, tell apart the information about the coefficients that you can know from the values at x=0, 1, −1 and the information you cannot know, find and fix an error in a solution, and show that several polynomials have the same information.
z-m-20-05.material: If you fully expand P(x)=(x²−x−1)³, it becomes a degree-6 expression with terms from x⁶ down to the constant term. Reading: P(x) is "x squared minus x minus 1, in parentheses, cubed". We want to get information about the coefficients without expanding. P(0), P(1), and P(−1) can easily be found by plugging directly into the parentheses. We will write the expanded expression as P(x)=a₆x⁶+a₅x⁵+a₄x⁴+a₃x³+a₂x²+a₁x+a₀ (reading: a₆ is "a six", and the number below is a name that shows the degree).
z-m-20-05.thinking.0: Interpreting which combination of coefficients the plugged-in value is
z-m-20-05.thinking.1: Finding and fixing the wrong line in a solution
z-m-20-05.thinking.2: Designing several polynomials that satisfy the same conditions
z-m-20-05.thinking.3: Explaining why the information is not enough
z-m-20-05.prereq.0: H1 in this task only marks the difficulty and support level of this production batch; it is not a grade placement in the curriculum. Assume you know middle school polynomial addition, subtraction and multiplication, the multiplication formulas, and basic factoring.
z-m-20-05.prereq.1: The meaning of the value when x=1, x=−1, x=0 are plugged into a polynomial (the value of a polynomial)
z-m-20-05.prereq.3: Solving simultaneous equations by adding and subtracting
z-m-20-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the things you can find using only the three values P(0), P(1), P(−1) (without expanding).
z-m-20-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write what value each term aₖxᵏ becomes when you plug in 0, 1, −1 for x, separating the case where k is even from the case where k is odd.
z-m-20-05.s.s1.hint.1: For each option, write which combination of the three values P(0), P(1), P(−1) gives that value, and if it cannot be expressed, make a counterexample with a simple polynomial.
z-m-20-05.s.s1.o.a: The value of the single coefficient a₃ of x³
z-m-20-05.s.s1.r.a: The three values are only information about certain sums of coefficients. You did not test whether the coefficient of one term can be known separately.
z-m-20-05.s.s1.r.b: This judgment looks at which term is left when you plug in 0 for x.
z-m-20-05.s.s1.o.c: The sum of the coefficients of the odd-degree terms
z-m-20-05.s.s1.r.c: This judgment sees how the signs of the odd-degree terms differ at x=1 and x=−1.
z-m-20-05.s.s1.o.d: The coefficient a₆ of x⁶ (the coefficient of the highest-degree term)
z-m-20-05.s.s1.r.d: You can tell the highest-degree term by looking at the structure of the expression, but these three values alone do not fix it. You did not distinguish what information the problem allows.
z-m-20-05.s.s1.o.e: The sum of all the coefficients
z-m-20-05.s.s1.r.e: This judgment sees that when you plug in x=1, every power of x becomes 1.
z-m-20-05.s.s1.explain: P(0)=a₀, P(1)=the sum of all the coefficients, and P(1)−P(−1)=2(the sum of the coefficients of the odd-degree terms). The coefficient a₃ of a single term or the coefficient a₆ of the highest-degree term is not fixed by these three values alone (if you look at the structure directly, you can see that a₆=1, but that is different information).
z-m-20-05.s.s2.prompt: A student found the sum of the coefficients of the even-degree terms and the sum of the coefficients of the odd-degree terms. Choose the one wrong line.
z-m-20-05.s.s2.hint.0: Subtract the expression with x=−1 plugged in from the expression with x=1 plugged in, and see directly which terms remain and which disappear.
z-m-20-05.s.s2.hint.1: Look at the coefficients in front of the remaining terms and compare them with the sum you want to find.
z-m-20-05.s.s2.line.3: Adding the two equations gives 2(a₆+a₄+a₂+a₀)=0, so the sum of the coefficients of the even-degree terms is 0.
z-m-20-05.s.s2.line.4: Subtracting the two equations gives that the sum of the coefficients of the odd-degree terms is (−1)−1=−2.
z-m-20-05.s.s2.explain: Line 5 is wrong. Subtracting the second equation from the first gives 2(a₅+a₃+a₁)=−1−1=−2, so the sum of the coefficients of the odd-degree terms is −1. Lines 1 to 4 are correct. The even-degree terms include the constant term a₀.
z-m-20-05.s.s3.prompt: For the cubic expression Q(x)=ax³+bx²+cx+d (a, b, c, d are integers, a≠0), make three different Q for which the sum of all the coefficients is 0 and the sum of the coefficients of the odd-degree terms is 2.
z-m-20-05.s.s3.hint.0: First choose a so that the sum of the two coefficients of the odd-degree terms is 2, and then match c.
z-m-20-05.s.s3.hint.1: Then calculate what the sum of the remaining two coefficients b and d must be for the sum of all the coefficients to be 0.

z-m-20-05.s.s3.explain: For example, x³+x−2 has coefficient sum 1+1−2=0 and the sum of the odd-degree coefficients is 1+1=2. 2x³−x²−1 also has sum 0 and odd-degree sum 2. There are several cubic expressions with the same two pieces of information.
z-m-20-05.s.s4.prompt: The different Q you made in s3 all have the same two pieces of information (coefficient sum 0, odd-degree sum 2). Write why these two pieces of information alone do not fix the cubic expression to one, and guess and write what more would be needed to fix it to one.

z-m-20-05.s.s4.model.0: There are four coefficients a, b, c, d, but there are only two equations, a+b+c+d=0 and a+c=2. So if you fix a, c follows, and b and d only have their sum fixed, so there can be many, like x³+x−2 and 2x³−x²−1. We need two more equations.
z-m-20-05.s.s4.model.1: The information is two sums, so each coefficient is not fixed. For example, if a=1 then c=1, and if a=2 then c=0, so different expressions come out. We need more conditions, such as the value of Q(2) or the value of a, and even then one more is needed to fix b and d.
